title: Cloud Computing
description: Cloud basics for the CISSP: characteristics, service and deployment models, virtualized compute, cloud identity, roles, protocols, migration, forensics and data destruction.

nodes.title: Characteristics
nodes.description:
Cloud is many different things to different people, so it is hard to define simply. Instead, the industry defines a set of characteristics: if a service has them, it is probably cloud.
There are five.

children.title: On-Demand Self Service
children.description:
Users request services, and the provider's software provisions them automatically, usually within milliseconds or seconds.
A huge shift from the old way: a 17-page form, approval in triplicate, then a 4 to 6 month wait for a new server.
Great for innovating, experimenting and failing fast. The dark side is shadow IT.

children.title: Broad Network Access
children.description:
Cloud resources are available from many device types and many locations.
The main way to access cloud services is a web browser over the internet. Almost everything has a browser and internet access, so you can reach cloud services from basically anywhere.

children.title: Resource Pooling
children.description:
A really important characteristic. The three primary resources are shared among many users:
- Compute: the ability to execute code (fetch, decode, execute and store).
- Storage: somewhere to keep the bits, both data and code.
- Network: the ability to move the bits around.
Users do not access the physical resources directly. A layer of virtualization sits in between: a virtual machine or container instead of a physical CPU, a virtual disk or object storage instead of a hard drive, a virtual switch instead of a physical one.
This sharing is what makes it easy to provision new services almost instantly, and to scale usage of compute, storage and network up or down quickly.

children.title: Rapid Elasticity
children.description:
Also called scalability: resources can be quickly provisioned and deprovisioned.
Need lots more bandwidth, or terabytes of extra storage? No problem. Scaling back down is just as easy.

children.title: Measured Service
children.description:
The provider closely monitors your usage, and you pay only for what you use.
Usage is monitored and reported to the consumer, which gives visibility and transparency of rates and costs.

nodes.title: Service Models
nodes.description:
The three most common types of cloud service: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Newer models fit between them: Containers as a Service sits between IaaS and PaaS, and serverless (Functions as a Service) sits between PaaS and SaaS.
For every service model it must be clear who is responsible for what. If responsibilities are not clearly defined, assume no one is doing it. You do not need to memorize the exact split for each model.
The onus is on the customer, who stays accountable for any data and services it outsources to the cloud. The customer must define responsibilities in contracts and SLAs, and make sure the provider's controls operate effectively. Assurance comes from service level reports or, more commonly, SOC 2 reports (covered in the first Domain 6 mind map).

children.title: IaaS
children.description:
Customers deploy virtualized servers, appliances, storage and networking components.
A customer can recreate an entire physical data center as virtual components: virtual firewalls, virtual routers, virtual servers and so on.

children.title: PaaS
children.description: Services and functionality for customers to develop and deploy their own custom applications, without worrying about the underlying servers, network and storage.

children.title: SaaS
children.description: The customer rents access to a complete application hosted in the cloud, and simply uses it.

nodes.title: Deployment Models
nodes.description: The major cloud deployment models: public, private, community and hybrid.

children.title: Public
children.description: Cloud services available to anyone. A cloud service provider owns and operates cloud infrastructure that is open to the general public.

children.title: Private
children.description:
Cloud infrastructure provisioned for the exclusive use of a single customer.
It can be owned and operated by the customer or by a cloud service provider, can be on or off premises, and can be physically or logically separated from other customers. It's complicated.

children.title: Community
children.description: Cloud infrastructure accessible only to a small community of organizations with similar shared concerns, such as similar security and regulatory requirements.

children.title: Hybrid
children.description:
Any combination of public, private and community cloud.
Example: a large organization has its own on-premises private cloud for sensitive data, and uses the public cloud for less sensitive data and workloads.

nodes.title: Virtualized Compute
nodes.description: In the cloud you usually have no direct access to physical servers and CPUs (see Resource Pooling). Instead you run your code and applications on virtualized compute: virtual machines, containers or serverless.

children.title: Virtual Machine
children.description:
An operating system and some applications running on a layer of abstraction, instead of directly on the physical hardware.
The physical server (CPU, RAM, network interface card and so on) is called the compute node. Several of them can run at the same time on one compute node.
On the exam, _____ may also be called instances or guests.

children.title: Hypervisor
children.description:
The software that provides the layer of abstraction between the hardware and the operating systems. Also called a VM monitor.
An operating system expects total control of the hardware, so two cannot normally share it. The _____ is a 'giant liar': it simulates the hardware for each OS, so each OS thinks it controls the hardware but really controls virtual hardware.
Know the difference between Type 1 (bare metal, runs directly on the hardware) and Type 2 (hosted, runs on top of an operating system) _____. Type 1 is more secure and efficient.

children.title: Containers
children.description:
Highly portable code execution environments that run within an operating system, sharing and using that operating system's resources.
Like the standard steel boxes of intermodal shipping: pack your code once, then run it anywhere without repacking, on a Mac laptop, an on-premises Linux server, the Azure cloud or Google Cloud.

children.title: Container Engine
children.description:
Containers also run on a layer of abstraction. The difference is where the layer sits:
- Virtual machines: between the hardware and the operating system.
- Containers: between the operating system and the containers.

children.title: Serverless
children.description:
More correctly called Functions as a Service.
Applications used to be monolithic: all functions packaged into one large executable, which is hard to scale. Microservices break the application into groups of functions that can be scaled separately. Functions as a Service goes further: the application is broken into individual functions that talk to each other through API calls.
Simple functions are written and stored in the cloud and called as much or as little as needed, a million times a second or once every three weeks. Developers basically do not have to think about infrastructure, and a function that is never called costs nothing.

nodes.title: Identity Provider
nodes.description:
The system that stores user identities and verifies who users are.
The cloud removes the traditional well-defined perimeter and trusted internal network. Identity is the new perimeter.
Assume all traffic is a potential threat, and verify every user thoroughly so you know exactly who is accessing what. This zero-trust approach needs very robust identification, authentication and authorization controls.
User identities can be stored in two main places: locally or in the cloud.

children.title: Local
children.description: Identities are stored in a system the organization maintains on premises, in its own data center. Usually Active Directory.

children.title: Cloud
children.description:
A service hosted by a third party on the internet stores the organization's user identities, so the organization does not run the system itself.
Example: Okta.

nodes.title: Cloud identity
nodes.description: How a user's identity for cloud services relates to their local identity. The types you can use: cloud, linked, synced or federated.

children.title: Cloud
children.description: An identity created and managed solely in the cloud.

children.title: Linked
children.description:
Two separate identities, one in the cloud and one local, with some indication that they are linked.
Changes to one are NOT automatically synchronized to the other.

children.title: Synced
children.description: Two identities, one in the cloud and one local, kept automatically in step. A change to one is automatically reflected in the other.

children.title: Federated
children.description: One identity that gives the user access to both local and cloud-based services through federated access.

nodes.title: Roles
nodes.description:
In the cloud it is critical to have clearly defined accountabilities and responsibilities.
Know the common parties involved, such as the consumer, provider, broker and auditor, and what each one is accountable or responsible for.

children.title: Accountable
children.description:
Ultimate ownership, answerability, blameworthiness and liability for an asset. The _____ person is the owner of the asset.
Assign this to only one person per asset: the throat that gets choked if something goes wrong.
It CANNOT be delegated. The _____ person sets the policies and requirements for protecting the asset, and delegates the work to others.

children.title: Responsible
children.description:
The doers: the person or people in charge of meeting the requirements set by the accountable person.
Multiple people can be _____, and this duty can be delegated.

children.title: Cloud Consumer
children.description: The customer: the person or organization using cloud services.

children.title: Owner / Controller
children.description:
People within the cloud consumer who are ultimately answerable for any data stored in the cloud. Also called data _____.
They are accountable for protecting the data they store and process in the cloud, and they stay accountable even when they outsource the data to a cloud provider.

children.title: Cloud Provider / Processor
children.description:
The company that runs the cloud services and handles consumer data on the consumer's behalf.
Responsible for protecting consumer data in the cloud, based on the requirements set by the data owner.
Accountable for running its own infrastructure and protecting its own data.

children.title: Cloud Broker
children.description:
Middlemen between the consumer and the cloud service provider.
They do aggregation, arbitrage and intermediation: packaging various cloud services together for a consumer, or adding functionality to a provider's offering.

children.title: Cloud Auditor
children.description: An independent party that examines cloud services to check whether controls are properly designed and operating effectively.

nodes.title: Protocols
nodes.description:
Protocols that enable identification, authentication and authorization in the cloud.
SAML, OpenID and OAuth all enable federated access, which is covered in more detail in the second Domain 5 mind map.

children.title: SPML
children.description:
An XML-based framework for exchanging provisioning information (setting up, changing and revoking access) between cooperating organizations.
It standardizes and simplifies provisioning access across multiple systems in multiple organizations.
Full name: Service Provisioning Markup Language.

children.title: SAML
children.description:
An XML-based standard that provides both authentication and authorization in federated access.
Full name: Security Assertion Markup Language.

children.title: OpenID
children.description: Provides only authentication.

children.title: OAuth
children.description: Provides only authorization.

nodes.title: Migration
nodes.description: Moving systems and data to the cloud raises many security questions: access controls, confidentiality, integrity and availability of the data, portability, interoperability, reversibility, resiliency, compliance and more.

children.title: Data Centric
children.description: Focus on the data to be migrated: its classification, and so the security controls needed at each stage of the data lifecycle: creation, storage, use, sharing, archiving and destruction.

children.title: SLA
children.description:
An important contractual tool for communicating the consumer's requirements to the provider.
Documented commitments by the provider to the consumer, covering things such as confidentiality, integrity, availability and responsiveness.
_____ are addendums to the overall contract.
Full name: Service Level Agreement.

nodes.title: Forensics
nodes.description: Investigating incidents and collecting evidence in the cloud, especially the public cloud, brings significant challenges as well as opportunities.

children.title: Snapshot, Virtual Disk, Image
children.description:
Sources of evidence in the cloud, from most to least useful:
1. Snapshot: a copy of a VM that preserves its state and data at a specific point in time. A primary source of evidence.
2. Virtual disk (VM volume): holds a lot of data, but none of the volatile data in the CPU cache, registers or RAM that a snapshot captures.
3. Image: a pre-built VM. Useful to find vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, but it holds none of the data of the running system.

nodes.title: Data Destruction
nodes.description: Defensible _____ is a challenge in the cloud. Many laws and regulations require the data owner to get rid of sensitive data, especially personal data, permanently, defensibly and demonstrably.

children.title: Crypto Shredding / Crypto Erase
children.description:
A way to defensibly destroy data in the cloud.
Encrypt the sensitive data with an excellent algorithm such as AES, then securely destroy every copy of the encryption key.
With no way to recover the key, the data is unrecoverable, so it has been defensibly destroyed.
